doc_summary: The paper introduces 'control evaluations', where a red team builds attack policies for an untrusted model (GPT-4) and the blue team's protocols are judged on worst-case safety versus usefulness in an APPS code-backdooring testbed. It also stresses that synthetic test inputs must be indistinguishable from real ones, or an adversarial model can exploit the difference.

items.claim: In a setup, make synthetic test inputs match the surface features of real inputs (theming, named characters, flavor text) instead of dryly describing the task, because a model that can tell synthetic from real inputs can behave well only on the synthetic ones.
items.quote: Our initial attempt at constructing synthetic inputs produced inputs that are easy to distinguish from real APPS problems. Real APPS problem descriptions usually have some flavor text with named characters

items.claim: In a setup, distort real observations so they resemble the synthetic ones (as well as improving the synthetic ones), because shrinking the distinguishability gap from both sides makes eval-vs-deployment detection harder.
items.quote: Distorting observations: Instead of running the monitor on real inputs, run it on inputs that have been distorted by asking $T$ to make them look more like the synthetic inputs, as suggested by Christiano, (2016).

items.claim: Prefers testing safety against a red-team attack policy that actively exploits the protocol's weaknesses over testing with the honest model's behavior, because safety must hold even when the model is intentionally subverting.
items.quote: We call this methodology for estimating the safety of a protocol, where the scenario is simulated using a red-team-provided implementation for the untrusted model, a control evaluation.

items.claim: Treats the model's ability to recognise that it is in a safety evaluation as the core bottleneck for the validity of evaluations, since it could sandbag when playing the attack policy.
items.quote: the untrusted model will know that it’s in a safety evaluation so it might intentionally play dumb while being used as an attack policy. Models purposefully failing at tasks is known as “sandbagging”.

items.claim: Reasons about detecting synthetic inputs as a Bayesian problem: at larger scale, the prior that any given input is synthetic rises, so a given tell stops enabling the model to behave differently across eval and real.
items.quote: the likelihood ratio stays the same but the prior that the input is synthetic goes up. And so, for any particular collusion signal, at some scale of scenario that collusion signal fails to allow effective collusion.

items.claim: Prefers worst-case (a single failure counts) safety metrics over average performance because rare catastrophic actions are what matter.
items.quote: Note that our safety property here involves taking the worst-case performance over the course of the scenario, rather than the average: it’s a safety failure if even one backdoor is submitted.

items.claim: Distrusts results from iterating and evaluating on the same problem set, flagging overfitting risk and the need for held-out validation.
items.quote: We iterate on prompts and techniques using the same 1500 APPS problems on which we evaluate safety and usefulness, which puts us at the risk of overfitting

items.claim: Chooses testbeds with deliberate properties (a capability gap, working auditing, and a non-trivially-solved baseline) so that the experiment is informative about protocol differences.
items.quote: We picked our setting to have the following properties: GPT-4 was much better at the problem than GPT-3.5, auditing malign GPT-4 submissions with GPT-4 worked well, and trusted monitoring didn’t totally solve the problem.

items.claim: Calls for future control evaluations in more complicated and realistic situations, with heterogeneous tasks and auditing failures that the toy setting did not model.
items.quote: We are excited about future work demonstrating these evaluations and techniques in more complicated and realistic situations.

items.claim: Prefers running evaluations in a secure environment without real useful-work affordances over deployment-like access, because the eval doesn't need dangerous affordances.
items.quote: During the evaluation, we aren’t trying to get the model to do actual useful work, and so the model doesn’t need to have access to dangerous affordances.
